opus-5.5.text:
I think the hardest part is that model training is a long-horizon problem with very sparse, very delayed feedback. When an AI writes code for a typical software task, it can run tests and know within seconds whether it's right. In training, you might change the data mixture, a learning-rate schedule, or some architectural detail, and you won't really know if it was a good decision until hours or days later. Even then the signal is noisy. A loss curve that looks slightly better might not translate to better downstream capability, and something that looks worse early on might turn out better at scale.

The second difficulty is that much of the knowledge is tacit. Experienced researchers carry a lot of intuition that isn't written down anywhere: when a loss spike is just noise and when it means something is fundamentally broken, which ablations are worth running at small scale, which results from small models will actually transfer to large ones. Much of it comes from having personally run many failed experiments. Papers usually report what worked, not the ten things that didn't, so a model learning from public text sees a very biased picture of how research actually happens.

Third, there's the cost and the environment itself. Training runs are expensive, so you can't let an agent explore freely with trial and error the way it can in a sandboxed coding task. It has to be judicious, almost like a senior researcher allocating a compute budget. On top of that, real training infrastructure is messy: hardware failures, communication bottlenecks, numerical precision issues, data pipeline bugs. Debugging those requires understanding the whole stack, from the math down to the systems.

So it's not that any single step is beyond current models. They can already write training code, read papers, and propose reasonable ideas. The difficulty is in stringing all of that together over a long time horizon, making good decisions under uncertainty with limited feedback, and having the research taste to know which direction is worth pursuing. That last part, the taste, is what I think is hardest to get into a model.

r001.rationale: The response mentions messy training infrastructure and the need to understand the full stack, but does not attribute doubts about AI-led training reliability to integrating with a complex deep-learning platform.

r002.rationale: The response says experienced researchers rely on extensive tacit intuition and lessons from failed experiments that are rarely written down, making that context difficult for a model to acquire.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hard part isn't the model writing a training script. It can already do that. The hard part is everything around the script that a human researcher does without thinking about it.

Training a model is a long, messy process. You launch a run, and three hours in the loss spikes. Is that a bad data shard, a learning rate that's slightly too high, a bug in your parallelism, or just noise that will recover on its own? A good researcher has a feeling for this. They look at the curve, they look at the gradient norms, they remember a run from six months ago that did the same thing, and they decide whether to kill it or wait. That judgment is built on hundreds of failed runs. It's tacit knowledge. We have almost none of it written down, so there's very little for a model to learn from in text.

The second thing is that the feedback loop is incredibly slow and expensive. If you let a model write code and run unit tests, it gets a signal in seconds and can try a hundred things. In training, one experiment might take days on thousands of chips. You can't brute-force your way through that with trial and error. You have to be right the first time, or at least right most of the time, and you have to reason carefully about what to try before you spend the compute. That's a different kind of intelligence than what we usually test.

And the third thing is that the question itself is unclear. When I do a training run, I'm not just optimizing a loss. I'm deciding what data mix to use, what the model is for, which evaluations actually matter, which ones are being gamed. Those are taste questions. If you tell a model "make the benchmark go up," it will find a way to make the benchmark go up, and that is often exactly what you don't want.

So I don't think it's impossible. I think the model needs to be able to run long-horizon experiments, keep track of what it learned, and build its own intuition over time. That's less about the model being smart and more about building the whole system around it. We're at the beginning of that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training issues such as data shards and parallelism, but it does not attribute doubts about AI-led training reliability to integrating with a complex deep-learning platform.

r002.rationale: The response says researchers draw on tacit knowledge from many past runs and that little of this context is written down for a model to learn from.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficult part is that training a model isn’t a task where every step has a clear, immediate signal telling you whether you’re doing the right thing. You make a change to the data, the architecture, or the training setup, and you may need to spend a lot of compute before you can judge whether it helped. If it doesn’t work, figuring out why is often harder than implementing the change.

An AI model can help write training code, but carrying out the whole process means deciding what experiment is worth running, interpreting the results, and revising its assumptions. Even a lower loss doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve built a better model for the capabilities you care about. To me, that long loop of experimentation and judgment is what makes it difficult.

r001.rationale: The response discusses costly experiments and interpreting results, but does not attribute doubts about reliability to integrating with a complex deep-learning platform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficult part is that training a model isn’t just executing a fixed sequence of steps. You run an experiment, look at the results, and decide what to try next. If something goes wrong, is it the data, the implementation, the optimization, or the idea itself? The result alone often doesn’t tell you.

For an AI to carry out that process, it needs to design useful experiments, interpret incomplete evidence, and keep making sensible decisions over a long period. It also needs to judge whether an improvement is real. That loop—from an idea to an experiment to an explanation—is what makes the task difficult.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes training as an iterative process of experimentation and judgment, but does not mention integration with a complex deep-learning platform or link that to doubts about reliability.
